note: Juno, queen of the gods and wife of Jupiter, took revenge on the women her husband loved and on their families. The canto opens with two tales of madness from Ovid's Metamorphoses, one from Thebes and one from Troy, to measure the frenzy Dante is about to see.
Semele was a princess of Thebes, loved by Jupiter and mother of the god Bacchus. Juno tricked her into her death, then turned on the rest of the royal house.
A king married to Ino, Semele's sister, who had nursed the infant Bacchus. Juno drove him mad, so that he took his wife and sons for a lioness and her cubs.
The second son, Melicertes. Ino leapt with him from a cliff into the sea.
Queen of Troy, wife of King Priam. After the city fell she was carried off as a slave by the Greeks, having seen her husband and most of her children killed.
Hecuba's daughter. The Greeks sacrificed her on the tomb of Achilles.

Hecuba's youngest son, sent away for safety to the king of Thrace with a store of gold. The king murdered him for it and threw the body into the sea. Virgil tells part of the story in the Aeneid, and Dante recalls it in Inferno 13.
In Ovid, Hecuba's grief turns her into a dog. Dante keeps her human and has her only bark: her mind is gone, not her shape.

The second kind of falsifier: those who passed themselves off as someone else. They pretended to be another person, and now they are out of their own minds, running rabid and biting whatever they meet.

context: He was still speaking to Dante at the end of Canto 29 when the mad soul seized him.
Capocchio's companion from Canto 29, left alone and afraid he will be bitten next.

note: A Florentine of the Cavalcanti family, dead by 1280 and famous as a mimic. The trick described below is the plot of Puccini's comic opera Gianni Schicchi (1918).

A princess of Cyprus in Ovid's Metamorphoses, who fell in love with her father, King Cinyras. She came to his bed in the dark, passed off as another woman. When he found out she fled, and was changed into the myrrh tree. Her child was Adonis.

A rich Florentine of the Donati family, into which Dante married. The early commentators tell that when Buoso died, a relative, Simone, hid the death and had Gianni Schicchi get into the bed and dictate a will in the dead man's voice. Gianni took care to leave something to himself.
The finest animal in Buoso's stables, a mare or a mule according to the commentators. It was the prize Gianni willed to himself.
A huge round belly with a thin neck and small head, like the body and neck of a lute. Without his legs, Dante says, the likeness would be complete.

Dropsy is a swelling of the body with fluid, and it brings a raging thirst. It is the punishment of the counterfeiters, the third kind of falsifier. They swelled good coin with base metal, and now their bodies are swollen with corrupt fluid.
A counterfeiter burned alive in Florence in 1281. "Master" is a title of learning or skill. Early commentators call him Adam of Brescia, but a document of the time suggests he was an Englishman.
An echo of the rich man in the Gospel parable, who begs from Hell for one drop of water to cool his tongue (Luke 16).
The Casentino is the upper valley of the Arno, in the mountains east of Florence. Dante knew it well: he fought there at the battle of Campaldino in 1289, and stayed there during his exile.
His memory is made part of his punishment. The cool streams where he committed his crime are always before his eyes, and the thought of them parches him more than the disease.
A castle in the Casentino, held by a branch of the Guidi, the great counts of that region. Its ruins still stand.

The gold florin of Florence, first struck in 1252, had John the Baptist, the city's patron saint, on one side and the Florentine lily on the other. It was pure gold and trusted across Europe. To debase it was to strike at the city's wealth and good name.
The Guidi counts of Romena, who set Master Adam to work. The unnamed brother is usually taken to be Aghinolfo. They were never punished. Dante later had dealings with this family in his exile.

Usually taken as Fonte Branda, the famous fountain of Siena. Others point to a spring of the same name that once ran near Romena. Either way: he would give up a drink of water, the thing he wants most, to see them suffer.
Guido, who died in 1292. The others were still alive in 1300.
Half the twenty-two miles of the ditch before (Inferno 29). The ditches of Malebolge shrink as they near the center.
A true florin was 24 carats, pure gold. Master Adam's were 21 parts gold and 3 parts cheap metal.
After judgment the damned fall to their place in Hell (Inferno 5).

quote: the lying woman who accused Joseph
note: The wife of Potiphar, an Egyptian officer. Joseph, sold into slavery by his brothers, served in Potiphar's house. She tried to seduce him, and when he refused she accused him of trying to rape her. He was thrown into prison (Genesis 39).

The Greek who let the Trojans capture him and swore that the wooden horse was a holy offering they should bring inside their walls (Aeneid 2). "The Greek from Troy" is a sneer: a Greek known only for what he did to Troy.
The punishment of the fourth kind of falsifier, the liars: a fever so hot that they steam.

What follows is a slanging match in the style of the comic insult poems of Dante's day, each speaker capping the other's taunt. Dante had written such verses himself, in an exchange of sonnets with his friend Forese Donati.
The condemned were led to the stake with their hands tied.
In the Aeneid, King Priam asks the captured Sinon to tell the truth about the horse. Sinon swears by the gods and lies.
Sinon told one lie. Every false coin Adam struck was a separate crime.
The hollow wooden horse filled with Greek soldiers, by which Troy was taken.
Water. In Ovid, the beautiful youth Narcissus fell in love with his own reflection in a pool and wasted away beside it.

context: Virgil is angry that Dante is enjoying the quarrel. Since Dante the poet wrote every word of it, the rebuke falls on him twice.

quote: Like someone who dreams of disaster
note: A dreamer in a nightmare wishes he were dreaming, and he is. In the same way Dante, too ashamed to speak, wishes he could apologize, and his silence is the apology.

quote: The desire to hear such things is base
note: One of the poem's well-known closing lines. Looking at sin in order to understand it is the purpose of the journey. Lingering over it for entertainment is a fault.
